concept.body: A composition is an assembly line: the first motion's OUTPUT is the second motion's INPUT. Never apply both to the original point — walk one point through station 1, take what comes out, and only then hand it to station 2.

explanationVariants: Station 1: (1, 2) → (4, 2). Station 2 doubles nothing — it reflects over the y-axis: (−4, 2).
Track the x: 1 → 4 after the slide, then the mirror flips it to −4.

widget.prompt: Take (1, 2). Apply (x, y) → (x + 3, y), then reflect the result over the y-axis. What is the final x-coordinate?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 is the x after the slide — the mirror hasn't acted yet. It flips the sign: −4.
−1 reflects the ORIGINAL point instead of the slid one. The mirror receives (4, 2), so it returns (−4, 2).

steps.body: Functions chain — so transformations do too. A **composition** applies one motion, then feeds its OUTPUT into the next: translate, THEN reflect. Because each rigid motion preserves distances and angles, any chain of them is still one rigid motion. Bookkeeping tip: track ONE point at a time through the chain.
Two slides, one shape — find the single motion that does both jobs at once.

widget.prompt: The dashed target is the triangle after sliding by (2, 1) and then by (3, −2). Land it with ONE slide.
widget.successFeedback: One slide of (5, −1) — exactly (2 + 3, 1 + (−2)). Composing translations just adds their components.
widget.offsetFeedback: Right shape, wrong parking spot: the two slides ADD component by component — dx = 2 + 3 = 5, dy = 1 + (−2) = −1.
widget.reflectFeedback: The copy is flipped — but both given motions were slides, and no chain of slides can reverse a shape's orientation. Turn the reflection off and translate only.

predict.prompt: After two translations, what single motion can always replace them?

options.label: One translation whose vector is the component-wise sum
A reflection followed by a smaller slide

predict.reveal: Translations compose by adding horizontal components and vertical components; orientation and all distances stay fixed.

cml.actionGoal: Compose two translations by moving one figure while coordinates and orientation update together.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Turn reflection on after matching the target. Which invariant breaks even though the figure can still look similar?

explanation.prompt: Why can one translation replace the two given translations?

options.label: Their displacement vectors add component by component.
options.feedback: Exactly—the net horizontal and vertical changes are vector sums.

options.label: The triangle changes shape to absorb the second move.
options.feedback: Translations preserve shape; they do not absorb displacement by deforming.

options.label: Every composition must pass through the origin.
options.feedback: The origin is not special; only the net displacement matters.

explanationVariants: Step 1: (7, 2) → (4, 2). Step 2, the 180° flips both signs: (−4, −2). The x-coordinate is −4.
Chain the rules: x goes 7 → 7 − 3 = 4 → −4 under the sign flip.

widget.prompt: Take (7, 2). Apply (x, y) → (x − 3, y), then rotate the result 180° about the origin. What is the final x-coordinate?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 is the x after the translation only — the half turn hasn't fired yet. 180° flips the sign: −4.
−10 comes from rotating FIRST ((7,2) → (−7,−2)) and translating after (−7 − 3 = −10). The given order is translate, THEN rotate: −4.

steps.body: **Order can matter.** Reflect-then-translate and translate-then-reflect are DIFFERENT functions in general — like putting on socks and shoes. Some pairs do commute (two translations always do), but never assume it: check by pushing a test point through both orders.

explanationVariants: Order A (reflect, then translate): (1, 3) → (−1, 3) → (3, 3). Order B (translate, then reflect): (1, 3) → (5, 3) → (−5, 3). Different outputs — the motions don't commute.
The reflection flips whatever x it receives; feeding it x = 1 versus x = 5 must end differently. One test point settles it.

widget.prompt: Motion R = reflect over the y-axis; motion T = (x, y) → (x + 4, y). Starting from (1, 3), do R-then-T and T-then-R land in the same place?

options.label: They differ: R-then-T gives (3, 3) but T-then-R gives (−5, 3)
options.feedback: Traced both ways the outputs disagree — this pair does not commute, so order is part of the composition's identity.

options.label: Same place — motions can be applied in any order
options.feedback: Trace it: R-then-T ends at (3, 3); T-then-R ends at (−5, 3). One test point is enough to sink "any order".

options.label: Same place, because both motions are rigid
options.feedback: Rigid protects DISTANCES, not order. Both orders give rigid results — just different ones: (3, 3) vs (−5, 3).

options.label: They differ, but only because rotations are involved
options.feedback: There's no rotation here at all — a reflection and a translation already refuse to commute: (3, 3) vs (−5, 3).

steps.body: One composition earns its own name: a **glide reflection** — a translation followed by a reflection over a line PARALLEL to the slide (footprints in snow: step forward, mirror to the other foot). Together with translations, rotations, and reflections, that completes the full cast of rigid motions.

widget.prompt: Left and right footprints alternate along a straight walking line — each print is the previous one slid forward AND mirrored across the line. Which single named motion carries one print to the next?

options.label: a glide reflection
options.feedback: Slide-along plus mirror-across-the-same-line is exactly the glide reflection — one named motion doing both jobs.

options.label: a translation
options.feedback: A pure slide would keep every print on the SAME side — all left feet. The prints alternate sides, so a mirror is involved.

options.label: a reflection
options.feedback: A pure mirror would put the next print directly ACROSS, not forward — the walk also advances, so a slide is involved.

options.label: a rotation
options.feedback: A turn would tilt each print at a new angle — these prints all point the same way down the path.

explanationVariants: Slide: (1, 2) → (5, 2). Mirror over the x-axis: (5, −2). The y-coordinate is −2.
Glide bonus: because the slide runs PARALLEL to the mirror line, this pair commutes — mirror-first gives (1, −2) → (5, −2), the same place.

widget.prompt: Glide reflection: apply (x, y) → (x + 4, y), then reflect the result over the x-axis. Starting at (1, 2), what is the final y-coordinate?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 is the y after the slide alone — the mirror hasn't fired. The x-axis flips it: −2.
5 is the final X-coordinate (1 + 4). The question asks for the y, which the mirror flips to −2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The slide leaves y at 2; the x-axis mirror flips it: −2.

hints: Run the first motion alone: what does y = x do to (2, 6)?
The swap gives (6, 2). Now the half turn acts on THAT point.
180° flips both signs of whatever it receives.
explanationVariants: Compose the rules: (x, y) → (y, x) → (−y, −x); at (2, 6) that's (−6, −2).

widget.prompt: Take (2, 6). Reflect over the line y = x, then rotate the result 180° about the origin. Final position?

options.feedback: Swap first: (6, 2). Then both signs flip: (−6, −2).
The swap got skipped — this is the 180° acting on the ORIGINAL point. The reflection hands the rotation (6, 2), not (2, 6).
(6, 2) is the point after the swap only — the half turn still has to flip both signs.
Only the x flipped — that's a y-axis reflection standing in for the rotation. A 180° turn negates BOTH coordinates of (6, 2).

takeaways: A composition feeds one motion's output into the next — and rigid chains stay rigid.
Order can matter: test a point through both orders before assuming it doesn't.
Glide reflection = slide + mirror over a line parallel to the slide — the last rigid motion in the cast.
steps.teaser: Next: point a motion back at its own figure — when does a shape map exactly onto ITSELF?
